entries.answer: C++ is an extension of C that adds classes, templates, automatic memory management and a much larger standard library, and it is the language behind most video games, desktop applications and much of the machine learning tooling. It is multi-paradigm rather than purely object-oriented, so you can write in an object style, a functional style or plain procedural code within the same program, and since it compiles to native machine code the performance ceiling is high when a bottleneck is reached. The cost of that power is complexity: a beginner can be overwhelmed by the number of features, and even experienced programmers spend years learning which ones to avoid. It is a compiled language, so the build step and header files are part of the workflow, and the language keeps changing, with new editions standardised roughly every three years.

patterns: what is a template in c++
why are template errors so long
entries.answer: A C++ template is a blueprint that generates a whole family of functions or classes from a single source definition, which is how the language achieves generic programming without a separate generic syntax. When you write a template on a type parameter and then call it with an int and a string, the compiler produces two separate real implementations, one for each type, and the original definition is not code you can call on its own. The consequence is that template errors often surface at the point of use rather than at the point of definition, with messages running to dozens of lines deep through the standard library, which is the single most complained-about aspect of the language. Templates also increase compile time and binary size, because the body is duplicated for every instantiation, and the idiom of putting all template definitions in a header exists only because the compiler must see them. The same mechanism powers the containers in the standard library, which is why a vector of one element type performs as well as an array.

patterns: what is the difference between unique ptr and shared ptr
entries.answer: A smart pointer is a class template in C++ that owns the object it points at and manages its lifetime automatically, and it is the answer to nearly every question about when to delete something. A unique_ptr models strict single ownership: it holds the object exclusively, it is movable but not copyable, and when it goes out of scope the object is destroyed. A shared_ptr models shared ownership with a reference count, so the object dies when the last shared_ptr holding it does, and a weak_ptr refers to a shared_ptr without adding to the count, which is what you use to break a reference cycle. The rule of thumb is to default to a unique_ptr and treat the existence of a shared_ptr as a design smell, because a cycle between two shared_ptrs leaks both objects permanently and no destructor will ever run. The older raw pointer syntax is still the easiest way to hand a non-owning observer, and the mistake is writing delete at all in new code.

entries.answer: Resource acquisition is initialization, usually shortened to RAII, is the C++ idiom in which every resource beyond memory is tied to the lifetime of an object so that releasing it cannot be forgotten. An object that owns a file, a lock, a socket or a transaction releases it in its destructor, and because destructors run when scope ends for any reason, including an exception or an early return, the cleanup happens automatically. This is the general principle behind smart pointers, and it is why std::lock_guard replaced manual lock and unlock pairs that could be skipped when an exception was thrown between them. The pattern is easy to state and easy to get subtly wrong: releasing in a copy constructor or assignment operator, for instance, breaks the guarantee and creates a double release, and knowing which operations acquire and which release is part of understanding the idiom. Its real payoff is that cleanup correctness stops being something you review line by line.

entries.answer: Object oriented programming is a way of organising a program around data that carries both state and the functions allowed to act on that state, rather than around a list of procedures. A class describes the shape of that data, an object is one concrete instance, and encapsulation means the outside world manipulates the object through its methods instead of writing its fields directly. The four ideas usually attached to it are abstraction, which hides detail behind a simple interface, inheritance, which lets one class reuse and specialise another, polymorphism, which lets one call site handle different concrete types, and composition, where a class holds another rather than deriving from it. The honest modern position is that inheritance is used far less than beginners expect: most real designs lean on composition, because deep hierarchies are expensive to change and are the main source of fragile base-class problems.
